Setup

Get from an empty window to a working agent, then learn the one habit every example uses: plan first, approve, then act.

Do it now in VS Code

  1. Open a new window. File > New Window.
  2. Install the GitHub Copilot extension. Open the Extensions view (Ctrl+Shift+X), search for GitHub Copilot, and install it. Sign in to GitHub when asked.
  3. Open a folder. File > Open Folder, then pick the folder that holds your course files. Here it is LIVE-DEMO.
  4. Save it as a workspace. File > Save Workspace As. Ours is 0-start-here/LIVE-DEMO.code-workspace.
  5. Open Copilot Chat and pick a model. Ctrl+Alt+I opens the chat. Choose Ask, Plan, or Agent, then a model.

Add extensions as needed: Python, Markdown tools, database tools. Extensions are apps for VS Code. Copilot is one of them.

Open AGENTS.md in DriveOpen the workspace fileFull setup guide

New slide · Setup, optional

Add more agents and models

Models: the brain

  1. Included. Click the model name in the chat box and pick another. Nothing to install.
  2. Another provider. Model picker > Manage Language Models > Add Models. Enter that provider's API key. You pay that provider.
  3. Local. Install Ollama and its VS Code extension. Your text stays on your machine.

Agent mode needs a model that supports tool calling.

Agents: the workers

  • Add other agents from the Extensions view: Claude (Anthropic), Codex (OpenAI), and other AI extensions.
  • Most read AGENTS.md too. Claude also reads CLAUDE.md.
  • Same workflow, different brain: plan, approve, execute, review.
How to add modelsVS Code: language models

How every example runs

1

Plan

The agent inspects the files and proposes concrete steps. Nothing changes yet. Every prompt here says STOP and wait for approval.

2

Approve

You read the plan. Approve it, or ask for a revision and get a new plan. The page has a Copy approval button for each one.

3

Execute

In Agent mode it carries out the approved work. Read the actual permission requests: a mode's label is not an approval policy.

4

Review

Read the changed files and the diff. Check the output. Ask for a report. Accept, revise, or restore a checkpoint.

Update the syllabus for Spring 2027

Same prompt, two agents: Claude and Gemini.

1Problem

Every semester I rebuild the syllabus by hand. New term, new lecture section, seven lab sections with new rooms, and a schedule where every date moves. One wrong date or grading weight reaches every student.

The task: turn the Fall 2026 Word syllabus into Spring 2027 from the official calendar and the section schedule, and keep every policy and grading weight.

Plan: Create the PetVax normalization lab walkthrough

Status: Awaiting instructor approval Working folder: G:\My Drive\0-Projects\!-important\data-book\publishing\Cengage\cce-2026\LIVE-DEMO\3-lesson-plan

Use a single visit with multiple treatments to show why a repeating cell is hard to query. Expand it into one treatment line per row. Explain why the catalog price and a line's actual charge belong in different tables.

For each action, provide the instructor cue, the Access menu or design-view steps, useful SQL, an expected result, and a checkpoint answer. Append parent records before dependent rows. Create the fictional example as live-normalization-unnormalized.csv and live-normalization-1nf.csv in the output folder. 1Problem

I have a semester of class-form submissions and want a quick, presentation-ready report. I gave the same prompt to Claude and to DeepSeek, on the same file. I got two different reports.

The point is not which model wins. It is how each one grouped the answers, and what that does to the numbers.

Complete prompt
GoalWhat I want and the role
Analyze the supplied BITM330 Fall2026.csv and produce a self-contained HTML report that works offline.
ContextWhere to work and what to read
Treat one record as a form submission, not a unique student.
TaskWhat to do, in order, with the approval stop
Use five sections: (1) submissions per session, (2) attendance-status responses overall and by session, (3) instructor question groups and categorized answer counts, including the practice-test yes/no question, (4) aggregate absence-reason categories, and (5) data-quality findings. Inspect the file first. Define and document every grouping rule and denominator. Do not infer why sessions have few responses. Do not reproduce personal responses or absence explanations. Preserve the CSV unchanged.
OutcomeWhat to save and report
Save the analysis plan, reproducible code, computed aggregate results, and a work report. Verify totals and explain any difference between initial expectations and computed results.

Claude

Plan: Quick data analysis of BITM330 Fall 2026 attendance log → HTML report

Context

Nim wants a presentation-ready analysis of G:\My Drive\0-Projects\!-important\data-book\publishing\Cengage\cce-2026\examples\data-analysis\BITM330 Fall2026.csv, output as an HTML file, with everything saved in a new claude\ subfolder next to the CSV. This sits in the CCE 2026 examples/ tree, so it doubles as a demo of an AI agent doing a data-analysis task for academic work.

What the data is (from inspection, read-only)

  • 2,436 Google-Form-style responses, 9 columns, no name/ID columns.
  • One row per student per class session. 8 real sessions (8/25 → 9/29/2026), roughly 250–320 rows each.
  • Columns: Timestamp, Date of Class, Class number, Attendance status, Why missed (free text, 14 rows), Seating (filled only on 9/29, n=283), Participation (n=288, multi-select ;-joined), Class question (free text), Your answer (free text).
  • Attendance: 2,408 Present, 14 Partial, 14 Absent (98.9% present).
  • Submission hours cluster at 2 PM (1,211) and 4 PM (860), suggesting two sections or a two-part class.
  • Data-quality issues worth surfacing: ~60 rows where class number disagrees with the date's dominant class; ~20 rows with impossible years (2003–2007, 2027, 3026); 39 rows whose timestamp date ≠ Date of Class; 4 #NAME? Excel artifacts in answers; the same instructor question typed 4–6 different ways.

Privacy constraint

"Why did you miss class" contains health and family details (surgery, funeral, hospital, biopsy). The report must aggregate only (counts by category such as medical / athletics travel / family), never quote excuse text verbatim. Student free-text answers will also be summarized (counts, lengths, yes/no split), not reproduced at length. No names exist in the file, so no other FERPA exposure.

Deliverables (all in ...\examples\data-analysis\claude\)

  1. analyze.py — standard-library-only Python (csv, collections, datetime, json, html). No pandas (not confirmed installed; stdlib is sufficient). Reads the CSV, computes all figures, writes the HTML.
  2. BITM330-Fall2026-analysis.html — self-contained report: inline CSS, inline SVG charts, no CDN, so it works offline in a conference room. Light/dark aware, readable at phone width.
  3. analysis-plan.md — this plan, copied into the folder so the method is visible next to the output.
  4. report.md — detailed written report: every number the HTML shows plus the ones that did not fit on a slide (per-session table, normalized question list with counts, answer categories with counts, absence categories, the full data-quality inventory with row counts), method notes, and caveats. Aggregates only, no verbatim student text.
  5. README.md — one-paragraph index of the folder and how to re-run (python analyze.py).

Report structure (per Nim's scoping: these five sections only)

  1. Submissions per session (bar chart, 8 real dates): shows the drift from ~310 down to ~283.
  2. Attendance status (present / partial / absent): overall split plus a per-session breakdown.
  3. Class questions: top instructor questions after normalizing case, punctuation, and whitespace; answers shown as categorized counts only (for example yes / no / other for the yes-no question, and coarse themes for the open questions such as "AI use" or "readings"); no verbatim student text.
  4. Absence reasons: categorized counts only (medical / athletics travel / family / other).
  5. Data-quality notes: the mismatches listed above, framed as "what an agent catches in 30 seconds."

Footer: source file, generated date, method (stdlib script), one-line privacy statement. Dropped from the earlier draft: headline tiles, submission-hour histogram, seating × participation.

Before writing chart code, load the dataviz skill for palette/form guidance (it triggers on any chart).

Steps

  1. Create claude\ folder; write analyze.py.
  2. Run it; open the HTML; check all five sections render and numbers match the profiling above (2,436 rows; 2,408 present / 14 partial / 14 absent; 14 absence reasons; 8 real session dates).
  3. Confirm no verbatim excuse text or long student answers appear in the HTML (grep for "surgery", "funeral", "hospital", "biopsy").
  4. Check the page at ~400 px width for horizontal scroll, and in dark mode.
  5. Have analyze.py also emit report.md from the same computed figures, so the HTML and the report can never disagree. Copy this plan to analysis-plan.md. Write README.md.
  6. Re-read report.md once for the same privacy check as step 3.

Out of scope / not touched

  • Nothing in the cce-2026 git repo changes. The CSV is read-only.
  • Optional follow-up Nim may want: save the prompt as a .github/prompts/*.prompt.md file in the repo, per AGENTS.md's "where prompts live" rule. Not done unless asked.

DeepSeek

Analysis plan — BITM 330 form data, quick session analysis

Folder: examples/data-analysis/deepseek/ (Google Drive copy of the CCE 2026 project) Source data: ../BITM330 Fall2026.csv — 2,609 form submissions, 9 columns. Read-only; never modified, never copied into the public repo. Prepared: 2026-09-30. Approved by Nim (v2.1) before execution. Executed by analyze.py.

Purpose

A quick, presentation-ready analysis of the BITM 330 class form data for the CCE 2026 data-analysis demo. Five sections only, in this order:

  1. Submissions per session — bar chart over the 8 real (in-person) session dates; shows the drift from first to last session.
  2. Attendance status — present / partially present / absent, overall and per session.
  3. Class questions — the top instructor questions (normalized, case- and punctuation-insensitive), answer categories as counts only, and the yes/no split for the yes/no question.
  4. Absence reasons — categorized counts only.
  5. Data quality — "what an agent catches in 30 seconds" checklist with counts.

Outputs: report.html (presentation result) plus session-stats.csv and category-counts.csv (backing counts). analysis-notes.md records what was done after the run.

Definitions and rules

  • Unit: one form submission. No unique-student inference; no attendance-rate claims. Every figure is labeled as a share or count of submissions.
  • Real session dates: parseable 2026 dates with 50 or more submissions (expected: 8/25, 8/27, 9/1, 9/3, 9/8, 9/15, 9/22, 9/29). Dates with fewer rows are "stray" or "near-empty" and are listed in the data-quality section instead of the chart.
  • Near-empty meeting days: inferred from the weekday pattern of the eight sessions; calendar days fitting the pattern between the first and last session are checked, and those with ~no submissions are listed.
  • No corrections, no deduplication, no imputation. Identical rows are counted, not merged. Entry errors are surfaced, never fixed.
  • Question normalization: lowercase, apostrophes removed, other punctuation becomes spaces, whitespace collapsed. The label shown is the most common original spelling of the cluster. "Did not ask" / "no question" style entries are counted separately.
  • Answer categories: Yes / No / Unsure / Other / Blank, by keyword rules (priority: blank, unsure, yes, no). Counts only — answer text is never displayed.
  • Absence buckets: Illness / medical, Family / personal, Athletics / travel, Schedule / work, Other; first matching bucket wins. Counts only — reason text is never displayed.
  • Privacy: free-text columns (reason, question, answer) never appear as raw text in any output. Questions appear only as the top normalized clusters; the displayed labels are reviewed before release.

Method

Single stdlib-only Python script (analyze.py): reads the CSV as utf-8-sig with stripped header names, computes everything in one pass structure, asserts summation checks, writes the three outputs, and prints an ASCII-only run summary.

Expected shapes (expectations, not results)

  • ~2,609 rows; 8 real sessions; first-to-last drift roughly 310 -> 283.
  • Session 7 (9/15) unusually low (~151 seen in reconnaissance).
  • Three near-empty meeting days (9/10, 9/17, 9/24).
  • If the run shows different values, the report states the actual values. Expectations are cross-checks, never targets.

Verification

  1. Script exits 0; only this folder is written; source file hash unchanged.
  2. Summation checks: date buckets = 2,609; per-session attendance = submissions; question buckets = all rows; answer categories = cluster sizes; absence buckets = reasons provided + no-reason count = absences.
  3. Expected-vs-actual recorded (8 sessions; drift; 9/15; near-empty days).
  4. Privacy scan of all outputs for distinctive free-text tokens; zero hits.
  5. Offline check: no external references in report.html; opens via file://; light and dark themes defined.
  6. Repo untouched; nothing committed or mirrored.

Provenance

  • v2.1 scope approved by Nim on 2026-09-30 (single HTML report + plan + work report, everything in this folder; supersedes the earlier profile/completeness scope).
  • Produced for the CCE 2026 hands-on comparison exercise ("deepseek" folder).

Tips for advanced users

When a prompt works, keep it: instructions, saved prompts, skills, workflows, and more than one agent.

Tip

Use multiple agents for the same task

Have them check each other's plans and output. You have an army of agents. Use it.

1

Same prompt

Give two agents the same prompt and the same files. This page does it twice: Claude and Gemini on the syllabus, Claude and DeepSeek on the data.

2

Cross-check the plans

Before you approve, give each agent the other's plan and ask what it missed.

3

Compare the outputs

Where they agree, you gain confidence. Where they differ, trace the difference to a rule, like 253/283 against 244/262.

4

You decide

Agents review agents. You still approve. Delegate work, not responsibility.

The review prompt I used on the two data reports
Compare the saved Claude and DeepSeek reports against their documented methods. List agreements and differences in counts, denominators, grouping rules, missing values, chart design, and interpretation. Do not label one model more accurate without checking the underlying computation. For the practice-test comparison, explicitly distinguish all session answers from the selected question cluster. Count CSV records separately from physical lines. Preserve the reports and source data. Save a concise comparison and unresolved questions. For a small demonstration edit, make a separate report copy and change only one chart title; do not change its values or scale.
